title: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
author: Arthur Conan Doyle
setting: London and the home counties, with excursions to Herefordshire, Surrey and Hampshire
lengthNote: Twelve stories, each written to fill a single issue of a monthly magazine
openingLine: To Sherlock Holmes she is always the woman.
summary: Twelve cases written to a monthly deadline, and the book that taught detective fiction its shape: a client with a story they have already misread, a detective who reads the room instead, and a narrator who withholds. Doyle's London runs on railway timetables, newspaper advertisements and rented lodgings, and the crimes are mostly about money and respectability rather than murder. Four of the twelve end without an arrest.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
sourceText.note: Quotations are placed by story. Standard Ebooks prints 'The Redheaded League' where most editions print 'The Red-Headed League'; the stories are otherwise in their magazine order.

atAGlance.label: Serialised
atAGlance.note: One story a month in The Strand Magazine, illustrated by Sidney Paget.

atAGlance.label: Collected
atAGlance.note: Published as a volume by George Newnes, in the magazine's own order.

atAGlance.label: Narrator
atAGlance.note: Every story is his written-up account, which means every solution reaches the reader second-hand.

atAGlance.label: Endings
atAGlance.note: Holmes lets the culprit go, or declines to involve the police, in several of the twelve.

structure.label: A Scandal in Bohemia
structure.title: The one he loses
structure.summary: A king wants a photograph recovered; Holmes fakes a fire to make its owner reveal the hiding place, and Irene Adler, who has already recognised him in disguise, walks out of the country with it. The collection opens by showing the method working perfectly and still failing.

structure.label: The Red-Headed League
structure.title: An absurd job with a tunnel under it
structure.summary: A pawnbroker is paid handsomely to copy out an encyclopaedia because of the colour of his hair. The comedy of the premise is what stops the reader asking the only question that matters, which is what his assistant does in the cellar all day.

structure.label: A Case of Identity
structure.title: A fiancé who was never there
structure.summary: Mary Sutherland's suitor vanishes on the way to the altar. The solution turns on a typewriter's worn letters and on an income of a hundred a year, and Holmes finds that he can prove everything and prosecute nothing.

structure.label: The Boscombe Valley Mystery
structure.title: A dying man's words, misheard
structure.summary: A son is charged with his father's murder on the strength of an overheard cry. Holmes reads the ground instead of the testimony, and uncovers a history of blackmail carried from the Australian goldfields into an English estate.

structure.label: The Five Orange Pips
structure.title: The case that arrives too late
structure.summary: Seed pips posted from abroad precede three deaths in one family. Holmes identifies the organisation, works out the ship and its route, and the client is drowned before any of it can be used — the collection's one outright failure to protect.

structure.label: The Man with the Twisted Lip
structure.title: A respectable man and his other trade
structure.summary: A City gentleman disappears in an opium den above the river, and a hideous beggar is found in his rooms. The answer is an income: begging in the correct make-up pays better than journalism, and the two men are one.

structure.label: The Adventure of the Blue Carbuncle
structure.title: A hat, a goose and a stone
structure.summary: A battered hat and a Christmas goose lead Holmes through the poultry markets to a jewel worth a fortune. Having solved it, he opens the door and lets the thief run, on the grounds that the season and the man's terror have done the work of a court.

structure.label: The Adventure of the Speckled Band
structure.title: A locked room and a stepfather's estate
structure.summary: Helen Stoner's sister died two weeks before her wedding; Helen is now moved into the same bedroom, and is due to marry. The bell-rope that rings nothing and the ventilator that ventilates nothing point at a will, an income and a doctor with a menagerie.

structure.label: The Adventure of the Engineer's Thumb
structure.title: A night job with a hydraulic press
structure.summary: A young engineer is hired for an enormous fee to service machinery in the dark, discovers what it is really pressing, and escapes with a hand short of a thumb. It is the story in which Holmes arrives after everything and solves nothing in time.

structure.label: The Adventure of the Noble Bachelor
structure.title: A bride who leaves during the wedding breakfast
structure.summary: An aristocrat marries American money and the bride disappears before the meal. Holmes works it out from a discarded dress and a note written on a hotel bill, and the solution is a first husband rather than a crime.

structure.label: The Adventure of the Beryl Coronet
structure.title: A banker who accuses the wrong child
structure.summary: A coronet pledged as security for a loan is found broken in a son's hands. The father's certainty about which of the young people in his house is dishonest turns out to be the case's central error, and the physical evidence is a matter of what a piece of gold will and will not do.

structure.label: The Adventure of the Copper Beeches
structure.title: A governess asked to cut off her hair
structure.summary: Violet Hunter takes a post on conditions so strange she writes to Baker Street about them. She observes, records and reasons before Holmes reaches the house, and the collection ends with the countryside, not the city, named as the more dangerous place.

characters.name: Sherlock Holmes
characters.summary: He works for interest rather than money, refuses cases that bore him, and treats the law as one option among several. The stories are careful to show his conclusions resting on specialist knowledge, correspondence, disguise and paid informants as much as on the famous glance at a sleeve.
characters.clue: He keeps his tobacco in a slipper, can tell a man's trade from his cuffs, and once let a thief run out of the door on Christmas because gaol would have finished him.

characters.name: Dr John Watson
characters.summary: He decides what the reader is told and when, which makes him the collection's most important technical device. His admiration shapes every portrait of Holmes, and his bafflement is what keeps a chain of inference feeling like a story rather than a demonstration.
characters.clue: An army surgeon invalided home, newly married in the middle of the book, who turns his friend's demonstrations into the thing his friend claims to despise.

characters.name: Irene Adler
characters.role: Contralto, formerly of the Warsaw Imperial Opera
characters.summary: She recognises Holmes in disguise, follows him home in men's clothes to be certain, and leaves the country with the photograph and a better husband. Watson records that Holmes has kept her picture and stopped joking about the cleverness of women.
characters.clue: An opera singer who spots a disguised detective in the street, wishes him goodnight by name, and is on the boat train before he opens the hiding place.

characters.name: Mary Sutherland
characters.role: A typist with an income of her own
characters.summary: Her hundred a year from a New Zealand annuity is the whole engine of the plot, and she cannot see it because she has been taught to think of the money as her mother's. Holmes solves her case and then declines to tell her the answer.

characters.name: Helen Stoner
characters.role: Stepdaughter of Dr Grimesby Roylott, of Stoke Moran
characters.summary: She arrives at Baker Street before seven in the morning, shaking, with bruises on her wrist from the man she lives with. Her sister died two weeks before a wedding and she is about to be married herself, which is the arithmetic the case actually runs on.
characters.clue: She comes in grey, veiled and shivering, and says it is not the cold that is making her shake.
characters.firstAppearance: The Adventure of the Speckled Band

characters.name: Dr Grimesby Roylott
characters.role: Physician, formerly of Calcutta, of Stoke Moran
characters.summary: A doctor with a temper, a prison record and a will that pays him while his stepdaughters stay unmarried. Doyle makes him physically enormous and has him bend a poker in the sitting room, so that the eventual method — small, quiet and indirect — comes as a genuine surprise.
characters.firstAppearance: The Adventure of the Speckled Band

characters.name: Violet Hunter
characters.summary: She is asked to cut her hair, wear a particular blue dress and sit with her back to a window, and she does all three while keeping a record. By the time Holmes arrives she has found the locked wing, tested the length of the ladder and worked out roughly what is being concealed.
characters.clue: A governess who accepts a post with impossible conditions, sits where she is told, and quietly uses a hand-mirror to see what is behind her.
characters.firstAppearance: The Adventure of the Copper Beeches

characters.name: Neville St. Clair
characters.role: A gentleman of Lee, and the beggar Hugh Boone
characters.summary: A journalist who went out to research an article on begging, discovered how much better it paid than writing, and spent years changing his face in a room above an opium den. He is the collection's clearest statement that respectability is a costume with an income attached.
characters.firstAppearance: The Man with the Twisted Lip

characters.name: Jabez Wilson
characters.summary: A slow, red-headed, thoroughly ordinary man who is paid four pounds a week to copy out an encyclopaedia and never wonders why. His complete lack of curiosity is the mechanism of the crime, and Doyle makes him likeable enough that the reader shares it.

characters.name: Inspector Lestrade
characters.summary: He appears to be there to be wrong, but the stories are more careful than that: he brings official power Holmes does not have, makes arrests, and is generally right about who had the opportunity and wrong only about what it means.

themes.name: Seeing against looking
themes.summary: The collection's founding distinction is that everyone in it has the same evidence and only one person uses it. Holmes reads sleeves, boots, hats and mud, but the stories are honest that this is not enough on its own: he also writes letters, pays informants, consults reference books and puts on costumes.
themes.development: Stated flatly in the first story with the stair-count, tested when the method wins and loses in the same case, and handed to a client in the last story, where Violet Hunter does the observing herself.

themes.name: Justice and testimony
themes.summary: Holmes is not a policeman, and several stories end with him deciding that the law would produce the worse outcome. He releases a thief at Christmas, keeps a dead man's secret, tells a client nothing, and in one case can only tell a scoundrel to his face that nothing can touch him.
themes.development: The pattern hardens across the book: early cases end in explanation, later ones in a private verdict, until the reader has to weigh the detective's authority as well as admire his method.

themes.name: Respectability
themes.summary: What most clients are really protecting is a position: a photograph that would end a royal engagement, a son who must not be charged, a husband whose City friends must not learn where his money comes from. The crimes are frequently less shocking than the exposure they threaten.
themes.development: From a king's marriage in the first story to a banker's household name in the eleventh, the pressure is the same, and the last story moves it out of London to show that distance from neighbours makes it worse, not better.

themes.name: Class and money
themes.summary: Almost every case has a figure in pounds at its centre: four pounds a week for copying, a hundred a year from an annuity, seven hundred a year from begging, fifty thousand pounds against a coronet. Doyle's London is a place where an exact income explains a person's conduct more reliably than their character does.
themes.development: The money is comic in the early stories and lethal by the middle ones, where two wills and an annuity are motives for killing.

themes.name: Marriage as a market
themes.summary: Weddings in these stories are transactions with documents attached. A stepfather invents a fiancé to keep his stepdaughter's income at home; a doctor needs his stepdaughters unmarried; a peer marries American mining money; a bride walks out of her own wedding breakfast.
themes.development: The collection keeps returning to the moment just before or just after a marriage, which is when money moves and when someone therefore becomes dangerous.

themes.name: Disguise and the law
themes.summary: Faces are unreliable throughout: Holmes as a groom and as a clergyman, a stepfather in whiskers and tinted spectacles, a journalist in a beggar's greasepaint, a governess made to sit where her face cannot be seen. Identity in this book is something worn, and often something owned by somebody else.
themes.development: Disguise begins as Holmes's tool, becomes the criminal's method by the third story, and ends as a way of controlling other people's bodies at the Copper Beeches.

techniques.name: The chain of inference
techniques.definition: A conclusion presented as a series of small observations, each of which the reader is invited to check.
techniques.inThisBook: Doyle's trick is to show the links only after the effect: Holmes states the conclusion, is challenged, and then walks the reader back through boots, cuffs and postmarks, so surprise and explanation arrive in that order.

techniques.name: Retrospective narration
techniques.definition: An account given after the event by a narrator who already knows how it ends.
techniques.inThisBook: Watson is writing these up from notes, sometimes years later, and says so. He therefore controls the order of disclosure completely — the reader learns what Holmes noticed at the moment Watson chooses to record it.

techniques.name: Disguise
techniques.definition: A character adopting another identity in full view of the audience.
techniques.inThisBook: Holmes goes out as a drunken groom and comes back as a Nonconformist clergyman; the collection's two best-hidden criminals are also in make-up, which puts detective and quarry in the same trade.

techniques.name: Frame narrative
techniques.definition: A story enclosed within another story, often several layers deep.
techniques.inThisBook: Most cases contain a long uninterrupted first-person account by the client, inside Watson's account, inside the collection — and the client's version is always the one with the mistake in it.

techniques.name: The misdirecting detail
techniques.definition: A conspicuous fact placed where the reader will take it for the important one.
techniques.inThisBook: The absurdity of the Red-Headed League occupies all the attention the cellar should be getting; a gypsy band, a dying man's last word and a hat left in the street work the same way.

techniques.name: Idiolect
techniques.definition: Giving each character a distinct and consistent way of speaking.
techniques.inThisBook: Holmes talks in imperatives and epigrams, Watson in careful subordinate clauses, and the clients in the vocabulary of their trade — a pawnbroker, a banker and an engineer each describe the same city in different nouns.

quotations.text: To Sherlock Holmes she is always the woman.
quotations.speaker: Dr Watson
quotations.context: The first sentence of the collection.
quotations.analysis: The present tense is the surprising part: Watson is writing long afterwards and the habit still holds. Naming her by a definite article rather than a name turns a person into a category of one, and the sentence works as an announcement that the book will begin with the case its hero lost.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'A Scandal in Bohemia'

quotations.text: He was, I take it, the most perfect reasoning and observing machine that the world has seen, but as a lover he would have placed himself in a false position.
quotations.speaker: Dr Watson
quotations.context: Watson explaining what Irene Adler did and did not mean to Holmes.
quotations.analysis: 'I take it' is a hedge, and it is Watson's, not Doyle's: the narrator is offering an assessment he cannot verify about a man he lives with. The machine image will be contradicted within twenty pages by the same narrator noticing that Holmes has kept a photograph.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'A Scandal in Bohemia'

quotations.text: You see, but you do not observe. The distinction is clear.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Before the stair-counting demonstration, in the sitting room at Baker Street.
quotations.analysis: The two verbs are almost synonyms in ordinary use, and Holmes prises them apart to make an ability sound like a discipline anyone could acquire. It is also a piece of self-promotion aimed at the man who writes the accounts, which is how the phrase came to be repeated for a century.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'A Scandal in Bohemia'

quotations.text: It is a capital mistake to theorise before one has data. Insensibly one begins to twist facts to suit theories, instead of theories to suit facts.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Refusing to speculate about an anonymous note before reading it properly.
quotations.analysis: The second sentence is the useful one, and it describes an error of character rather than of method — 'insensibly' concedes that nobody notices themselves doing it. Doyle, trained as a doctor, is describing diagnosis, and the collection's guilty parties are usually people who decided early what a fact meant.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'A Scandal in Bohemia'

quotations.text: I am lost without my Boswell.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Stopping Watson from leaving as a client arrives.
quotations.analysis: He does not say he needs an assistant; he says he needs a biographer. The joke concedes the whole structure of the book — that Holmes's work only exists for us because a companion writes it up — and it flatters Watson at the exact moment Holmes wants him to stay.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'A Scandal in Bohemia'

quotations.text: And that was how a great scandal threatened to affect the kingdom of Bohemia, and how the best plans of Mr. Sherlock Holmes were beaten by a woman’s wit.
quotations.speaker: Dr Watson
quotations.context: The closing sentence of the first story.
quotations.analysis: Watson gives the defeat the cadence of a triumph, with the long balanced clauses of a case closed. Note what the sentence does not say: the photograph is still in Adler's keeping, and the only thing actually recovered is Holmes's opinion of women.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'A Scandal in Bohemia'

quotations.text: It is quite a three pipe problem, and I beg that you won’t speak to me for fifty minutes.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: In the stalls at a concert, before the night's work at the bank.
quotations.analysis: Thinking is given a unit of measurement and a duration, which is a very Victorian way of describing genius — as a quantity of labour rather than a flash. The fifty minutes also buys Doyle a scene break, and the reader is kept outside the reasoning until the cellar.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'The Redheaded League'

quotations.text: My life is spent in one long effort to escape from the commonplaces of existence. These little problems help me to do so.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: After the arrest, yawning, as the case ends.
quotations.analysis: The motive stated here is not justice, money or curiosity but boredom, and it is offered as the ordinary condition of his life rather than an affectation. 'Little problems' reduces a bank robbery and a ruined pawnbroker to a distraction, which is the coldest thing Holmes says in the collection.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'The Redheaded League'

quotations.text: Depend upon it, there is nothing so unnatural as the commonplace.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Arguing that ordinary life is stranger than anything a novelist would invent.
quotations.analysis: It inverts the usual defence of realism: the commonplace is not the safe ground but the anomaly. Placed at the head of the collection's least violent case — a stepfather in false whiskers protecting an annuity — the remark functions as a working instruction for reading the rest.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'A Case of Identity'

quotations.text: The law cannot, as you say, touch you
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: To James Windibank, having proved that he courted his own stepdaughter in disguise.
quotations.analysis: He concedes the legal point and then, in the same breath, tells Windibank that no man ever deserved punishment more, before reaching for a hunting crop. The story ends with the crime proved, the criminal untouchable and the victim never told — a combination Doyle repeats often enough that it cannot be an accident.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'A Case of Identity'

quotations.text: There is nothing more deceptive than an obvious fact
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: On the train to Herefordshire, discussing the case against young McCarthy.
quotations.analysis: The line sets up the story's mechanism exactly: a son quarrels with his father, the father is found dead, and everybody stops there. Doyle is describing how circumstantial cases are built, and the story that follows is really about the difference between what happened and what a jury would believe.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'The Boscombe Valley Mystery'

quotations.text: You know my method. It is founded upon the observation of trifles.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Explaining to Watson how he read the ground by the pool.
quotations.analysis: 'Founded upon' is a builder's phrase, and the claim is that the small things are the foundation rather than the ornament. The sentence is also a piece of brand management — Holmes speaks of his method as an established system, to a man whose published accounts are what established it.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'The Boscombe Valley Mystery'

quotations.text: None of those which come to me are. I am the last court of appeal.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Answering a client who says his case is no ordinary one.
quotations.analysis: He describes himself in the language of a legal hierarchy while standing entirely outside it, and the claim is about position rather than skill: people reach him when the institutions have already failed. The story then makes the boast unbearable, since this client is dead within hours.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'The Five Orange Pips'

quotations.text: It was only by trying begging as an amateur that I could get the facts upon which to base my articles.
quotations.speaker: Neville St. Clair
quotations.reference: The Man with the Twisted Lip
quotations.context: Explaining how a journalist came to spend years as a beggar in the City.
quotations.analysis: The word 'amateur' is the hinge: he begins as a professional writer imitating a beggar and ends as a professional beggar imitating a gentleman, and the change is measured only in income. Doyle lets the man tell it himself, so the reader gets the whole social argument in the voice of someone who would rather not be making it.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'The Man with the Twisted Lip'

quotations.text: My name is Sherlock Holmes. It is my business to know what other people don’t know.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.reference: The Adventure of the Blue Carbuncle
quotations.context: To a salesman in the Covent Garden market, having just won a bet about geese.
quotations.analysis: Two flat declarative sentences, one giving a name and one giving a trade, as though the second followed from the first. 'Business' is doing a lot of work: knowledge is stock, and the scene he has just played out was a small commercial transaction conducted with a sovereign and a wager.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'The Adventure of the Blue Carbuncle'

quotations.text: I suppose that I am commuting a felony, but it is just possible that I am saving a soul.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.reference: The Adventure of the Blue Carbuncle
quotations.context: After letting James Ryder run out of the door at Christmas.
quotations.analysis: He names his own offence accurately and in legal language, then sets a soul against it on the other side of a 'but'. The balance of the sentence is the whole of his private jurisdiction: a man with no warrant weighing a prosecution against a life, and telling only Watson.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'The Adventure of the Blue Carbuncle'

quotations.text: It is not cold which makes me shiver
quotations.speaker: Helen Stoner
quotations.reference: The Adventure of the Speckled Band
quotations.context: At Baker Street before seven in the morning, moved nearer the fire.
quotations.analysis: Holmes has offered a physical explanation and she corrects it, which is the first sign that this client can be relied on to report accurately. Doyle gets a whole atmosphere out of a denial: the word 'terror' is never needed because the body has already supplied it.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'The Adventure of the Speckled Band'

quotations.text: When a doctor does go wrong he is the first of criminals. He has nerve and he has knowledge.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.reference: The Adventure of the Speckled Band
quotations.context: Discussing Dr Grimesby Roylott with Watson, himself a doctor.
quotations.analysis: The observation is made to a physician by a man whose own qualifications are the same two — nerve and knowledge — which places Holmes and Roylott uncomfortably close together. Doyle had been a practising doctor, and the remark reads as a professional's assessment of what his training would equip him to do.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'The Adventure of the Speckled Band'

quotations.text: Violence does, in truth, recoil upon the violent, and the schemer falls into the pit which he digs for another.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.reference: The Adventure of the Speckled Band
quotations.context: Standing over Roylott's body with the snake still in the room.
quotations.analysis: He reaches for a proverb and a psalm at the one moment in the collection where he has actually caused a death, and the borrowed wisdom does the work of not saying so. Holmes admits privately afterwards that he is indirectly responsible and that it will not weigh heavily on him.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'The Adventure of the Speckled Band'

quotations.text: I have lost my thumb and I have lost a fifty-guinea fee, and what have I gained?
quotations.speaker: Victor Hatherley
quotations.reference: The Adventure of the Engineer's Thumb
quotations.context: On the train back to London, the house burnt and the gang gone.
quotations.analysis: He totals the case as a balance sheet and finds it in deficit, which is the only story in the collection to end that way. Holmes answers 'Experience', and the joke does not quite cover the fact that the detective arrived after everything and caught nobody.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'The Adventure of the Engineer’s Thumb'

quotations.text: It is very good of Lord St. Simon to honour my head by putting it on a level with his own
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.reference: The Adventure of the Noble Bachelor
quotations.context: After the departing aristocrat has said the case will need wiser heads than either of theirs.
quotations.analysis: The client intended a courtesy and has delivered an insult, and Holmes returns it by taking the words literally. It is the collection's sharpest joke about rank, made by a man who has solved the case before the peer finished stating it and who declines to be thanked for it.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'The Adventure of the Noble Bachelor'

quotations.text: No, the debt is not to me. You owe a very humble apology to that noble lad, your son, who has carried himself in this matter as I should be proud to see my own son do, should I ever chance to have one.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.reference: The Adventure of the Beryl Coronet
quotations.context: To Alexander Holder, who has had his son arrested for the theft.
quotations.analysis: The case is solved by physical evidence but judged on character, and the judgement falls on the client rather than the thief. The closing clause is the one glimpse of a private life the collection allows Holmes, and he offers it as a measure of someone else's conduct rather than a confidence.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'The Adventure of the Beryl Coronet'

quotations.text: I can’t make bricks without clay.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.reference: The Adventure of the Copper Beeches
quotations.context: Waiting for Violet Hunter's next letter, with nothing to work on.
quotations.analysis: He has just barked the same word three times, and the sentence that follows turns detection into a trade with raw materials and a supplier. The clay comes from a governess who is already inside the house, which makes her the working investigator of the story's first half.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'The Adventure of the Copper Beeches'

quotations.text: It is my belief, Watson, founded upon my experience, that the lowest and vilest alleys in London do not present a more dreadful record of sin than does the smiling and beautiful countryside.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.reference: The Adventure of the Copper Beeches
quotations.context: Looking out of a train window at isolated houses in Hampshire.
quotations.analysis: The reason he gives is not moral but architectural: isolation, and the impunity it grants. It closes the collection by reversing the expected geography of Victorian crime fiction — the city is dangerous because it is crowded, the country because nobody is near enough to hear.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'The Adventure of the Copper Beeches'

timeline.label: Arthur Conan Doyle born in Edinburgh
timeline.detail: Into an Irish Catholic family; he took his medical degree at Edinburgh University.

timeline.label: Doyle enters the Edinburgh medical school
timeline.detail: There he encountered Dr Joseph Bell, whose habit of diagnosing a patient's trade and travels from their appearance is the acknowledged model for Holmes's method.

timeline.label: A Study in Scarlet
timeline.detail: Holmes and Watson's first appearance, in Beeton's Christmas Annual, to very little notice.

timeline.label: The Sign of the Four
timeline.detail: The second novel, commissioned at a Lippincott's Magazine dinner in 1889 that also produced Wilde's The Picture of Dorian Gray.

timeline.label: The Strand begins the series in July
timeline.detail: 'A Scandal in Bohemia' appears with Sidney Paget's illustrations, and the magazine's circulation climbs with each number.

timeline.label: The twelve stories collected as a volume
timeline.detail: Published by George Newnes in October, in the order they had appeared.

timeline.label: Doyle kills Holmes at the Reichenbach Falls
timeline.detail: 'The Final Problem' closes the second series; readers cancelled subscriptions in numbers the magazine did not forget.

timeline.label: The Hound of the Baskervilles begins serialisation
timeline.detail: Set before the Falls, so that the detective could return without being resurrected.

timeline.label: Holmes brought back to life
timeline.detail: 'The Adventure of the Empty House' explains the Reichenbach disappearance and restarts the series.

timeline.label: The last Holmes story published
timeline.detail: The Case-Book closes a sequence of fifty-six short stories and four novels written across forty years.

timeline.label: Doyle dies at Crowborough
timeline.detail: By then better known to himself for his spiritualist writings than for the detective.

places.name: Baker Street, London
places.note: The consulting room every case passes through, and the fixed point the collection returns to twelve times.

places.name: Covent Garden
places.note: The poultry market where Holmes traces the goose that swallowed the blue carbuncle.

places.name: Upper Swandam Lane, by the Thames
places.note: The riverside district east of London Bridge where the opium den of 'The Man with the Twisted Lip' is placed.

places.name: Stoke Moran, Surrey
places.note: The Roylott house in 'The Speckled Band', set by Doyle on the western border of Surrey near Leatherhead.

places.name: Winchester, Hampshire
places.note: The city Holmes and Watson travel to in 'The Copper Beeches', looking out at the isolated houses that prompt his last speech.

places.name: Boscombe Valley, Herefordshire
places.note: The estate and pool of the Boscombe case, where the ground rather than the witnesses gives the answer.

criticalViews.position: The stories as the template for modern detective fiction
criticalViews.summary: The collection fixed a formula — eccentric amateur, admiring narrator, client interview, false solution, physical clue, explanatory speech — that most twentieth-century detective writing either follows or deliberately breaks.
criticalViews.counter: It risks treating Doyle as a machine for producing puzzles, when several of these stories have no crime, no arrest, or no solution that arrives in time.

criticalViews.summary: Criticism has long argued that the interest lies in the narration rather than the deduction: the reader's pleasure depends on a narrator who possesses the clues without understanding them, and whose affection colours every description of Holmes.
criticalViews.counter: Pushed far, it makes Holmes a projection, which the stories resist — his impatience with Watson's storytelling is one of their running jokes.

criticalViews.summary: Later readings attend to what the cases are about rather than how they are solved: annuities, wills, mortgages, professional respectability, the economics of begging, and the vulnerability of women who depend on male relatives for an income.
criticalViews.counter: Doyle is not a reformer, and the stories usually restore the arrangements they have exposed rather than question them.

essayQuestions.question: How important is Watson to the effect of the Holmes stories?
essayQuestions.focus: Narration, withholding and the reader's position
plan: Establish that every story is written up afterwards by a participant, and find the places where Watson admits to selecting.
Use the opening of 'A Scandal in Bohemia' to show how his admiration frames the portrait before any case begins.
Examine a demonstration scene — the stair count, the hat, the boots — and track exactly when the reader is given each fact.
Contrast with 'The Man with the Twisted Lip', where the client tells his own story and Watson steps back.
Conclude on the running joke that Holmes despises the stories his method depends on for its reputation.

essayQuestions.question: 'Holmes is a private authority answerable to nobody.' Discuss with reference to at least three stories.
plan: Count the outcomes: how many of the twelve end in arrest, and how many in a private decision.
Take 'The Blue Carbuncle' as the clearest case of mercy, and weigh the reasoning Holmes gives Watson for it.
Set against it 'A Case of Identity', where the law cannot act and Holmes also declines to tell the victim the truth.
Consider 'The Speckled Band', where his intervention causes a death he then judges in borrowed proverbs.
Decide whether the collection presents this authority as a solution to the law's failures or as a second problem.

essayQuestions.question: Examine the presentation of women in The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes.
plan: Begin with Irene Adler, who is introduced as an exception and defeats the method by using it.
Set the dependent clients — Mary Sutherland, Helen Stoner — beside the income or will that puts them in danger.
Use Violet Hunter, who investigates before the detective arrives, as the strongest counter-example.
Weigh Watson's habit of describing women's appearance first and their reasoning second.
Ask whether the collection admires independence or merely finds it striking.

essayQuestions.question: What does Doyle's London contribute to these stories?
essayQuestions.focus: Setting, anonymity and the machinery of a modern city
plan: Gather the infrastructure the plots run on: trains, cabs, post, newspapers, banks, lodging houses.
Show how the same systems that let Holmes move fast let criminals disappear — the beggar, the typewriter, the advertisement.
Consider class geography: Coburg Square, Harley Street, Swandam Lane and Lee are different economies as well as different addresses.
Turn to the final story's claim that the isolated countryside is worse, and test it against the rural cases.
Conclude on what the city does to identity when nobody's neighbours know them.

discussionQuestions: The collection opens with the case Holmes loses. What does beginning there do to everything that follows?
Watson keeps saying Holmes is a machine, and keeps recording evidence that he is not. Whose view should we take?
Four of the twelve cases end without anybody being charged. Is Holmes dispensing justice or avoiding it?
Violet Hunter does most of the observing in the last story. Does that strengthen the method or undermine the detective?
Nearly every case has an exact sum of money at its centre. What kind of society is being described?

related.why: The novel published a year earlier, where the same partnership is given room for a chase, a treasure and Watson's marriage.
The English detective novel Doyle inherited: a stolen jewel, multiple narrators and a professional detective who gets it wrong.
An earlier sensation novel built on the same Victorian fears — disputed identity, a woman's income, and documents that can be forged.
Published five years before these stories and set in the same fog: professional respectability with a second address behind it.
The decade's other bestseller about reading evidence — timetables, letters and phonograph cylinders assembled against something the law cannot charge.
